questions.title: Section A — Question 1 (Case study: daisy reproduction in the Succulent Karoo)

subQuestions.questionText:
The Source Material describes reproduction in Succulent Karoo daisies — sexual and asexual reproduction, floral structure, polyploidy, r-strategy seed production and 'aerial' seed banks. From the Source Material, give the scientific term for each description:
1.1.1 The process by which a plant grows from a seed into a seedling.
1.1.2 When the pollen from the anther is deposited on the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant.
1.1.3 A cell with two complete sets of chromosomes.
subQuestions.memoText:
1.1.1 Germination
1.1.2 Self-pollination
1.1.3 Diploid
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText: Many species of daisies occur in large numbers because they use a combination of sexual and asexual reproduction. Differentiate between pollination and fertilisation in flowering plants.
subQuestions.memoText:
Pollination (1): the transfer of pollen from the anther (of one flower/plant) to the stigma (of the same or another plant).
Fertilisation (1): the fusion of the male gamete (from the pollen grain) with the female gamete / egg (in the ovule).

subQuestions.questionText: Tabulate ONE difference between sexual reproduction and asexual reproduction of these daisy plants. No heading is required.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks (3): table drawn + column headings + one comparable difference. Examples:
Sexual reproduction | Asexual reproduction
Involves meiosis and fertilisation (fusion of haploid gametes) | No meiosis or fertilisation occurs
Offspring genetically different from the parent | Offspring genetically identical to the parent
Requires more energy (flowers, pollen, seeds produced) | Requires less energy (e.g. rhizomes produced)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why the asexual production of daisy family food crops, such as lettuce and artichokes, would be economically beneficial.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2, or 1 well explained (2 marks): it uses less energy (no energy spent on flowers or pollen) and is faster and easier; offspring are genetically identical to the parent, so desirable traits are retained and the product is uniform; it bypasses vulnerable juvenile stages; it gives larger, more predictable yields — more food and profit.

subQuestions.questionText:
Consider Figures 1.3, 1.4 and 1.5 (angiosperm and daisy floral structures). Identify the type of section shown of the daisy flower in Figure 1.4.
(Refer to Figure 1.4 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText: Longitudinal section.

subQuestions.questionText:
State the LETTERS and NAMES of the following parts of the angiosperm flower in Figure 1.3:
(a) The structure responsible for the production and release of male gametes.
(b) The female reproductive structure that receives the pollen grains.
(Refer to Figure 1.3 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) G — anther (2).
(b) A — stigma (2).
(letters as per the memo key)

subQuestions.questionText:
Calculate the magnification of the daisy pictured in Figure 1.4. The image size is about 80 mm and the actual size is 12 mm. Show all working.
(Refer to Figure 1.4 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size = 80 mm ÷ 12 mm = 6,67 × (accept a range of about 6,0–7,0 ×) (3 marks — formula + working + answer).

subQuestions.questionText:
Examine the male and female parts of the floret (Figure 1.5) and suggest why self-pollination is unlikely to occur in daisies.
(Refer to Figure 1.5 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText: 2 marks: the anthers are positioned well below the stigma, so pollen released from the anthers is unlikely to accidentally reach / touch the stigma of the same floret.

subQuestions.questionText: Polyploid daisy species are better able to cope with environmental change. Explain what is meant by 'polyploidy' in plants.
subQuestions.memoText: Having more than two complete sets of chromosomes (more than the diploid 2n number).

subQuestions.questionText:
(a) Name ONE reproductive advantage of polyploidy in daisies.
(b) Explain how this reproductive advantage would help the daisy to survive changing climatic conditions in the Succulent Karoo.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) (1): any one — larger seeds; more seeds; larger outer florets; larger flowers.
(b) (2): e.g. larger seeds → more stored nutrients → better seedling survival and a greater chance of coping with / outcompeting others under changing conditions; OR more seeds → a greater chance that some offspring land on suitable ground and germinate, so the population persists through change; OR larger outer florets → attract more pollinators → more pollination, fertilisation and seed set → the next generation survives the changed environment.

subQuestions.questionText:
Succulent Karoo daisy species hold back their seeds for extended periods until climatic conditions are favourable for germination.
(a) State whether these daisies use an 'r-' or 'K-' reproductive strategy.
(b) Give ONE piece of evidence from the text to support your answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) r-strategy (1).
(b) (1): 'a single daisy flower can contain as many as 2 000 florets, each with the potential to develop a seed' — very large numbers of offspring are produced.

subQuestions.questionText: Name the part of the flower from which the daisy seed develops.
subQuestions.memoText: The ovule.

subQuestions.questionText: Describe ONE benefit for a daisy plant of retaining seeds in an 'aerial' seed bank.
subQuestions.memoText: 1 mark: the seeds are protected and held until conditions are right (e.g. after rain / during the wet period), giving a much greater chance of successful germination and seedling survival.

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest and explain ONE way in which tourism could benefit from storing indigenous daisy seeds in seed banks.
subQuestions.memoText: One advantage + its benefit to tourism (2 marks), e.g.: a seed bank protects the variety of daisy species that draw tourists to the area; areas damaged by climate change or frost can be replanted so that the flowers still bloom in the tourist season; it preserves rare / endangered species that are a tourist attraction.

questions.title: Section A — Question 2 (Case study: elephant reproduction and population control)

subQuestions.questionText: The Source Material describes the African elephant — reproductive strategies, courtship, the menstrual cycle, immunocontraception and vasectomy as ways of controlling population growth. Explain why elephants are considered to be a 'problem' in South Africa.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): elephant numbers have increased / there is overpopulation in reserves; too many elephants damage large trees and other vegetation, which negatively affects the diversity and forage available to other animals.

subQuestions.questionText:
For each option (A to C) circle ONLY the term that applies to elephants:
A 'r-' reproductive strategy; 'K-' reproductive strategy
B ovipary; ovovivipary; vivipary
C external fertilisation; internal fertilisation
subQuestions.memoText:
A — 'K-' reproductive strategy
B — vivipary
C — internal fertilisation
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText: Identify ONE courtship stimulus employed by the African elephant and describe how this stimulus can assist in successful mating.
subQuestions.memoText: Name/describe a courtship behaviour (1) + its outcome (1). Examples: females make low-frequency rumblings to advertise their reproductive state and attract distant males; males release chemical signals (pheromones) in their urine or from head glands to show they are ready to mate; a receptive female holds her tail to one side / stands still to signal she will allow mounting; males in musth show dominance displays / mock battles / push over trees to demonstrate strength and pursue females; males raise their trunks to smell / detect the female's pheromones and assess her readiness.

subQuestions.questionText: Provide ONE piece of evidence from the Source Material to suggest that elephant mothers engage in long periods of parental care.
subQuestions.memoText: Any one (1 mark): they teach their calves everything (how to stand, swim, find food, protect themselves); they are fiercely nurturing and protective; they nurse their young for 4–6 years.

subQuestions.questionText: Elephant females experience a unique type of menstrual cycle. Describe ONE hormonal difference between the menstrual cycle of an elephant and a human.
subQuestions.memoText: Any one (1 mark): elephants have two LH surges per cycle whereas humans have one; in elephants LH levels are higher than FSH before and after ovulation, whereas in humans they are similar; the elephant LH surge occurs around day 9–10 versus around day 12–13 in humans.

subQuestions.questionText:
(a) Name the hormone responsible for the maintenance of pregnancy.
(b) Describe how this hormone maintains pregnancy.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Progesterone (1).
(b) (1): it maintains and thickens the endometrium (increases the blood supply / vascularisation of the uterine lining) so that the embryo/foetus can implant and develop.

subQuestions.questionText: Examine Figure 2.4 (the negative feedback mechanism controlling the menstrual cycle and the effect of immunocontraception). What is meant by the term 'negative feedback'?
subQuestions.memoText: 1 mark: when an increase in the level of one hormone causes a decrease / inhibition in the level or secretion of another hormone (bringing the system back towards its set point).

subQuestions.questionText:
Match the hormone in Column A with the appropriate function in Column B:
Column A: FSH; Oestrogen.
Column B: A Stimulates the development of secondary sexual characteristics; B Stimulates ovulation; C Stimulates the development of a follicle in the ovary.
(Refer to Figure 2.4 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText:
FSH — C (stimulates the development of a follicle in the ovary).
Oestrogen — A (stimulates the development of secondary sexual characteristics).
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText: Describe how the immunocontraceptive vaccine prevents pregnancy from occurring.
subQuestions.memoText: 3 marks (compulsory: antibodies): the vaccine stimulates the female to produce antibodies against the ovum's outer membrane (zona pellucida); these antibodies coat / block the egg so that sperm cells cannot penetrate it; fertilisation therefore cannot take place.

subQuestions.questionText:
Calculate the calving percentage, indicated by (A), for year 3 of the vaccine programme described in Table 2.1, where 7 calves were born to 50 vaccinated cows. Show all working.
(Refer to Table 2.1 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText: Calving % = (number of calves born ÷ number of cows vaccinated) × 100 = (7 ÷ 50) × 100 = 14% (2 marks — working + answer).

subQuestions.questionText:
How many years did it take for 100% sterilisation of vaccinated cows to be achieved?
(Refer to Table 2.1 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText: 4 years.

subQuestions.questionText: Identify ONE of the desired requirements for elephant contraceptives that is achieved by immunocontraception.
subQuestions.memoText: Any one (1 mark): long-term anti-fertility effect; little impact on secondary sexual characteristics; no health risk to the elephant; economically feasible; does not disrupt social group behaviour; easy to administer.

subQuestions.questionText: Surgical vasectomies have been performed on large dominant male elephants. What is a vasectomy?
subQuestions.memoText: 1 mark: the cutting / blocking / sealing of the sperm ducts (vasa deferentia) of both testes.

subQuestions.questionText: Why would a vasectomy leave a male sterile?
subQuestions.memoText: 1 mark: it prevents sperm from travelling from the testes into the semen, so no sperm are released during mating and fertilisation cannot occur.

subQuestions.questionText: Research shows that elephant vasectomies do result in behavioural changes. Suggest why sterilised males will still be able to engage in courtship behaviour.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 3 (3 marks): a vasectomy does not affect the pituitary's release of LH, which still stimulates the interstitial (Leydig) cells of the testes to produce testosterone; the incision does not cut the blood vessels to the testes, so testosterone production — which drives male courtship behaviour and musth — continues; the instinctive drive to mate is unaffected.

subQuestions.questionText: Provide ONE explained reason why 'inbreeding' would negatively impact the ability of elephant populations to adapt to changing climatic conditions.
subQuestions.memoText: One consequence + one linked explanation (2 marks): inbreeding reduces genetic diversity (and increases the expression of harmful recessive mutations / inbreeding depression); with less variation there are fewer alleles for natural selection to act on, so the population is less able to adapt quickly to the stressors of a changing climate.

subQuestions.questionText: Do you think the use of contraceptives to control elephant population growth is ethical? Provide reasons from the Source Material to support your answer.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 facts, or 1 well explained (2 marks). YES: it controls population growth and prevents further habitat and vegetation destruction; it is a non-lethal method causing less psychological harm than culling; it protects the biodiversity of elephant habitats; overpopulation would otherwise increase competition for space, food and resources. NO: it disrupts normal social and courtship behaviour; elephants should be allowed to live natural lives; there are long-term genetic risks (inbreeding, reduced adaptability); the procedures can cause stress and discomfort; the elephants cannot consent.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to Sources A–F in the Source Material Booklet (maternal age and pregnancy trends; pregnancy complications and figures on genetic defects, NICU admissions and term of birth; health risks to the reproductive and endocrine systems; parenting styles of older and younger mothers; effects on lifespan and offspring mortality; and effects on mental health). Consider the statement:

"Pregnancy at advanced maternal age causes more health risks for mother and child." (Advanced maternal age = women who are 35 years or older at the date of delivery.)

Using the source material and your own knowledge, discuss your opinion in an essay of 2½–3 pages. You are expected to: read the sources carefully; take a definite stand; plan your essay before writing (the plan is marked); present a debated argument using relevant information from Sources A–F plus your own Life Sciences knowledge; arrange the information to develop your argument; write in a scientifically appropriate way; and discuss at least nine different facts from the sources.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marked with the IEB essay rubric (40): Planning (6); Use of knowledge from sources (8); Use of own knowledge (4); Content relevance (2); Quality of argument supporting the decision (8); Fairness — counter-opinions integrated (4); Presentation (4); Scientific merit (4). Do not double-mark a fact used from more than one source.

Examples of usable facts —
FOR (advanced maternal age DOES raise risks): after 35, increased risk of miscarriage, genetic abnormalities, gestational diabetes and high blood pressure; after 40, higher chance of caesarean delivery, premature birth, low birth weight, birth defects and stillbirth (A); ~87% of oocytes are poor quality by age 32 and fertility declines from age 32 (A, Fig 3.1); chromosomal abnormalities rise (6,4%), and the 35–39 and 40+ groups show the highest proportion of genetic defects and higher pregnancy-complication and NICU-admission rates (B); 42–49-year-old mothers all had pre-term births, and 35+ shows a steep rise in the risk of foetal loss (B, Figs 3.3–3.4); ageing reproductive and endocrine systems bring declining progesterone and oestrogen, altered feedback sensitivity, insulin resistance and placental problems (praevia, detachment, uterine bleeding) (C); children of older parents carry more DNA mutations / impaired mitochondrial function and age faster (E, Fig 3.5), and face an increased risk of schizophrenia and higher depression/anxiety linked to parental frailty (F).
AGAINST: many women in their 40s still have healthy pregnancies, and fertility only truly ends after ~42 (A, Fig 3.1); birth rates for ages 35–39 rose 272% and 40–44 rose 318%, and one doctor argues age matters less than underlying health conditions (A); under-20s show the highest rates of congenital heart and nervous-system defects, and 18–24 and 34–44 childbirth-complication rates are similar (B, Fig 3.2); younger mothers have higher mortality rates and worse long-term health, and their children can show higher schizophrenia risk (E, F); older mothers are often more emotionally stable, mature, financially secure and better educated, and their children perform better academically, report better health and have fewer behavioural issues (D, F).
